title: Policy-as-Skill: Governed LLM Decision Support with Evidence, Deterministic Control, and Audit
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 22 Sep 2026]
    Title:Policy-as-Skill: Governed LLM Decision Support with Evidence, Deterministic Control, and Audit
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Organizations increasingly use LLMs for policy, compliance, risk, and operational decision support, requiring evidence validation, review routing, version control, and auditability. We introduce Policy-as-Skill (PaS), a modular runtime that packages these functions as executable, versioned policy capabilities. Thirteen methods are evaluated with a fixed Gemma4 backend on 600 development tasks. PaS+Audit achieves 53.8% exact accuracy, macro-F1 0.346, review F1 0.854, citation precision 1.000, policy-reference recall 0.984, and audit completeness 1.000, outperforming LLM+RAG on most governance and review metrics. Deterministic control raises aggregate accuracy to 61.2% but is strongly task dependent, supporting selective rather than universal rule-based intervention.

report.summary: Policy-as-Skill packages LLM governance functions—evidence validation, review routing, versioning, and audit—into versioned runtime skills, beating standard RAG on most compliance metrics.
report.background: Enterprises increasingly deploy large language models for policy interpretation, compliance screening, risk assessment, and operational decision support. These settings demand more than fluent answers: every recommendation must cite validated evidence, route uncertain cases to human reviewers, track which policy version was applied, and leave a reconstructable audit trail. Standard retrieval-augmented generation (LLM+RAG) helps ground outputs in documents but offers no built-in guarantees on citation precision, review routing, or audit completeness, and it is weak at enforcing versioned rules. Policy-as-Skill (PaS) responds by treating these governance functions not as prompt instructions but as modular, executable, versioned "policy capabilities" invoked alongside the model. The authors evaluate thirteen method variants using a fixed Gemma4 backend across 600 development tasks, directly comparing PaS configurations against a conventional LLM+RAG baseline on accuracy, review quality, citation, policy-reference, and audit metrics.
key_points: PaS reframes governance as executable infrastructure, not prompting. Evidence validation, review routing, version control, and audit logging are packaged as modular, versioned policy "skills" that a runtime invokes. This means a compliance rule can be updated, diffed, and rolled back like software, rather than living implicitly inside a system prompt or retrieval index.

PaS+Audit outperforms LLM+RAG on most governance and review measures. It reaches 53.8% exact accuracy, macro-F1 0.346, review F1 0.854, citation precision 1.000, policy-reference recall 0.984, and audit completeness 1.000. Perfect citation precision and audit completeness are the standout results: every answer was traceable and every decision reconstructable in the tested setting.

Deterministic control raises aggregate accuracy to 61.2%, but unevenly. Hard rule-based intervention lifted the headline number while remaining strongly task dependent, meaning some task types benefit greatly and others are hurt. The authors therefore argue for selective, not universal, rule-based override—routing only where rules are known to help.

Raw accuracy remains modest, so humans stay in the loop. A 53.8% exact-match rate and 0.346 macro-F1 indicate the system is not autonomously resolving policy questions. Its real strength is the review pipeline: high review-routing F1 suggests it reliably flags cases needing human judgment, which is often the practical bottleneck.

The benchmark is narrow but controlled. Thirteen methods were compared on a single fixed Gemma4 backend over 600 development tasks, isolating architecture effects from model choice. This strengthens internal comparisons but limits claims about generalization to other models, domains, or larger production workloads.
report.impact: For the AI industry, PaS signals that governance is becoming a first-class product layer rather than an afterthought bolted onto RAG. Perfect audit completeness and citation precision are exactly what regulated buyers—finance, healthcare, insurance, public sector—need before approving LLM deployment, which could push vendors to ship versioned policy skills, provenance tracking, and deterministic override hooks as standard features. For developers, the takeaway is architectural: separate evidence validation, routing, and versioning from the model, and treat rule-based control as a selectively applied tool rather than a universal layer. Expect more hybrid orchestrators that combine LLM reasoning with small deterministic policy engines. For regular users, the practical benefit is more consistent, cited policy answers and clearer escalation when confidence is low—though the modest accuracy means human reviewers remain essential, not optional.
report.tools: To follow up, explore policy-as-code engines (Open Policy Agent/Rego, AWS Cedar) for deterministic control; RAG and orchestration stacks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack); guardrail and routing libraries (Guardrails AI, NeMo Guardrails); citation and RAG evaluation (RAGAS, TruLens); and provenance/observability tooling (OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, MLflow). Watching whether the authors release PaS code or benchmark data would be the fastest way to reproduce selective deterministic intervention.
